title: Awful dizzy attacks: episodic vertigo with right ear symptoms in a 55-year-old woman in general practice
desc: This station involves a focused history and a focused ear and neurological examination of a 55-year-old woman in general practice who has had two attacks of spinning vertigo, each lasting about 8 hours, over 3 months. She also has fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness in her right ear, and she fears a brain tumour. The candidate then interprets her observations and audiology report, diagnoses Ménière's disease, and plans ENT referral, treatment for attacks, lifestyle measures, opportunistic preventive care (sexual health, smoking, cancer screening), safety advice about driving and red flags.
focus: Telling vertigo from other dizziness by its timing, triggers and ear symptoms, and diagnosing and managing Ménière's disease in general practice
diagnosis: Smoking, unprotected sex and cancer screening (opportunistic)
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a general practice. Kathy Smith, a 55-year-old woman, has come in complaining of dizziness. Your GP supervisor will see her after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mrs Smith and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Mrs Smith's observations and her audiology report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Kathy Smith, a 55-year-old receptionist. Today you feel completely well, between attacks, but the attacks frighten you and you are anxious. You live alone. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “I’ve just had these awful dizzy attacks recently.”

The dizziness (give only when asked):

  • What it feels like: “the room is spinning” around you. You do not feel faint or lightheaded and you have never blacked out.
  • How often and how long: twice in the last 3 months, and each attack lasted about 8 hours. Between attacks there is nothing at all: you feel normal. The most recent was about 2 weeks ago.
  • Onset: each attack came on out of the blue. The first came while you were watching TV one evening, and the second while you were cooking dinner.
  • Triggers: they are not brought on by turning your head, rolling over in bed, lying down or standing up.
  • Relief: lying still with your eyes shut helps a little. You took nothing for them.

Other symptoms: if the candidate asks an open question such as “Any other symptoms?”, reply “Like what?”. Give each of the following only when the candidate names it:

  • Hearing loss: yes, in the right ear. It is “terrible” during the attacks, and between attacks it has not been what it was.
  • Ringing in the ear (tinnitus): yes, a roaring in the right ear, worse during the attacks.
  • Fullness or pressure in the ear: yes, in the right ear, “like it needs to pop”, during the attacks.
  • Nausea and vomiting: yes, in both attacks. You vomited several times.
  • No ear pain or discharge.

Say no if asked about: shortness of breath, chest pain, palpitations, a recent cold or flu, fever, weight loss, headache, facial droop, numbness or weakness, double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, blackouts, a head injury, zigzag lights in your vision, or sensitivity to light or noise.

Past medical history: none. You have never had surgery.

Medicines: hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for 2 years. You are postmenopausal. No other medicines.

Allergies: none.

Family history: your mother had migraines and your father had high blood pressure. You have no siblings.

Social history:

  • Smoking: you recently started smoking again, about 10 cigarettes a day.
  • Alcohol: a glass of wine a night.
  • Coffee (only if asked): 3 or 4 cups a day at work.
  • Work and activity: you are a receptionist and drive to work (say so if asked about driving). You walk 3 times a week and cook for yourself.
  • Home: you live alone. You were recently divorced. When asked about home or relationships, say: “Since the divorce I’ve been dating again, a few different men.”
  • Sexual history (only if asked): since the divorce you have had several partners and have not used condoms.
  • Screening (only if asked): you are not sure when you last had a cervical screening test, a bowel screening test or a mammogram.

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • Concern (say this when asked what you are worried about): “I’m terrified it’s brain cancer.” You also dread having an attack at home on your own.
  • Expectation: you want to know what is causing the attacks and whether it is serious.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: “Could this be something growing in my brain?” Accept a brief answer, or a promise to come back to it once the results are back.

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: well-looking, comfortable, sitting steadily. Not pale.
  • Observations: the practice nurse has done them: all within normal limits, with no postural drop. (The full set is handed over in Part 2.)
  • Ears, inspection: normal pinnae, no scars, no discharge.
  • Otoscopy: both ear canals clear. Both tympanic membranes intact, pearly grey, with a normal light reflex. No fluid or retraction.
  • Whispered voice test (each ear tested with the other ear masked): reduced on the right, where she misses most of the number and letter combinations; normal on the left.
  • Rinne (512 Hz): positive in both ears: air conduction is louder than bone conduction.
  • Weber (512 Hz): lateralises to the left.
  • Eyes: no spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus. Eye movements full with smooth pursuit and no double vision. Head impulse test (if performed): normal to both sides, with no corrective saccade.
  • Cranial nerves V and VII: facial sensation normal in V1, V2 and V3 on both sides. Corneal reflex present (if mentioned). Facial movements full and symmetrical. The other cranial nerves are normal.
  • Limbs: tone, power, reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical.
  • Cerebellar: finger-nose, rapid alternating movements and heel-shin normal.
  • Gait: normal, including heel-to-toe walking. Romberg negative. Unterberger (if performed): no significant rotation.
  • Dix-Hallpike (each side): no nystagmus and no vertigo. Negative on both sides.
  • Heart and neck (if examined): heart sounds dual with no murmur. No carotid bruits.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Mrs Smith's identity, and explains the examination and gains consent.
Empathic and non-judgemental throughout: acknowledges her fear of brain cancer and of an attack while alone, explains why before asking about her sexual history, and uses plain language.
History
Characterises the dizziness:

kids.x: Nature: asks what she means by dizzy and establishes true vertigo (the room spinning), not lightheadedness or fainting.
Timing: two attacks in 3 months, each about 8 hours, completely well between them.
Triggers and relief: spontaneous, not brought on by head position, lying down or standing; lying still with her eyes shut helps a little.

check.x: Asks specifically about ear and associated symptoms:

kids.x: Hearing loss: right ear, terrible during attacks and not back to normal between them.
Tinnitus and fullness in the right ear; no ear pain or discharge.
Nausea and vomiting during the attacks.

check.x: Screens for neurological red flags of a central cause: headache, facial droop, numbness or weakness, double vision, slurred speech or trouble swallowing, loss of consciousness [all absent].
Screens other systems: chest pain, shortness of breath or palpitations, recent URTI, fever, weight loss [all absent].
check.d: Award only if at least two systems beyond the ears are screened.

check.x: Asks about migraine features and the family history: headache, visual aura, sensitivity to light or noise [none]; mother has migraines, father hypertension, no siblings.
Takes the past medical, medication and allergy history: no illnesses or surgery; HRT for 2 years, postmenopausal; no allergies.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking, alcohol and caffeine: recently restarted, about 10 a day; a glass of wine a night; 3 or 4 coffees a day.
Home, work and driving: lives alone, recently divorced, receptionist who drives to work, walks 3 times a week, cooks for herself.
Sexual history, asked sensitively: several partners without condoms.
kids.d: Award if the candidate follows up the cue sensitively (explains why, asks about partners and condom use).

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: terrified it is brain cancer, dreads an attack while alone, wants to know the cause and whether it is serious.
Examination
Asks for the observations, including lying and standing blood pressure [normal, no postural drop].
Inspects both ears and performs otoscopy on both sides [canals and tympanic membranes normal].
Performs a whispered voice test in each ear, masking the other ear [reduced on the right, normal on the left].
Performs tuning fork tests with a 512 Hz fork:

kids.x: Rinne in both ears [positive on both sides: air conduction louder than bone].
Weber [lateralises to the left], and states that with a positive Rinne this means a right sensorineural hearing loss.
kids.d: Award only if the side and the type of loss are both correct.

check.x: Examines eye movements and looks for spontaneous and gaze-evoked nystagmus [full movements, no nystagmus]; a head impulse test, if performed, is normal.
Examines cranial nerves V and VII: facial sensation, corneal reflex and facial movements [normal].
Examines for a central cause: cerebellar signs, gait, heel-to-toe walking and Romberg, and states they would complete the limb neurological examination [all normal].
Performs or offers the Dix-Hallpike test on both sides [negative].
check.d: Also award if the candidate states it is not indicated because the vertigo is not positional.

check.x: Interpretation
Interprets the observations as normal: no postural drop and a normal glucose, so no orthostatic or metabolic cause, and the symptom is vestibular rather than presyncope.

Interprets the audiogram as a right low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (no air-bone gap; 35 to 40 dB worse than the left at 250 and 500 Hz), with a mild symmetrical high-frequency loss in keeping with age, and links it to the Weber result.

Interprets the speech and middle ear tests: good word recognition on the right, type A tympanograms and present acoustic reflexes favour an inner ear (cochlear) cause; notes the audiologist's advice that an asymmetric loss needs ENT review and consideration of an MRI.

Gives Ménière's disease of the right ear as the most likely diagnosis, justified by two or more spontaneous attacks of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, a documented low-frequency sensorineural loss in that ear, and fluctuating hearing, tinnitus and fullness in that ear.

Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: vestibular migraine, BPPV, vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis, vestibular schwannoma, and posterior circulation TIA or stroke.
check.d: Award for at least three, including vestibular schwannoma and a central (vascular) cause, each justified.

check.x: Management
Explains the diagnosis to Mrs Smith in plain language and checks her understanding:

kids.x: An inner ear disorder (too much fluid pressure in the hearing and balance organ) causing attacks of spinning, hearing loss, ringing and nausea; the cause is unknown.
Most likely an inner ear condition, not a brain cancer; because the hearing loss is one-sided, ENT may arrange an MRI to rule out a rare, non-cancerous growth on the hearing nerve.
There is no cure, but treatment controls the symptoms, and the hearing in that ear can become permanently worse over time.

check.x: Refers to ENT (non-urgent) with the audiogram; explains that ENT may arrange an MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a vestibular schwannoma; does not order a CT brain.
Advises lifestyle measures: a low-salt diet, limiting caffeine and alcohol, and stopping smoking.
Plans medicines:

kids.x: For attacks: prochlorperazine (for example 5 to 10 mg orally up to three times a day), short courses only.
kids.d: Accept the drug and short-term use without the exact dose.

kids.x: For prevention: betahistine or a diuretic may be tried, usually on ENT advice, though the evidence is limited; intratympanic or surgical options are reserved for attacks that do not respond.

check.x: Addresses opportunistic preventive care:

kids.x: Sexual health: advises condoms and offers STI testing.
Smoking: brief advice to quit, offers Quitline referral (13 7848) and pharmacotherapy, and books a dedicated cessation appointment.
Checks that her cervical screening, bowel screening and mammogram are up to date.

check.x: Safety netting

Names red flags in plain words: call 000 for weakness or numbness, a drooping face, slurred speech, double vision or trouble walking; same-day GP or ED for a sudden drop in hearing in either ear that does not recover, or vomiting with no fluids kept down.
check.d: Award for at least two stroke symptoms with 000, and sudden hearing loss with same-day review.

check.x: Gives safety advice for attacks: sit or lie down straight away, keep a phone nearby as she lives alone, and do not drive (or climb or swim alone) while an attack could start; fitness to drive is reviewed once the attacks are controlled.
check.d: Advising her to arrange other transport to work until the attacks are controlled is good practice but not required for the mark.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: STI results followed up by phone or a short visit within a week; GP review in about 4 weeks with a symptom diary; ENT appointment.

part2.lead: Here are the practice nurse's observations from this morning, and the report of the hearing test Mrs Smith had this afternoon at the audiology service in the same medical centre; she has come back to discuss the results.
part2.patient:
• When the candidate explains the diagnosis, ask: “So it’s not a brain tumour? Why would I need a scan, then?” Settle if the candidate explains honestly and kindly.
  • Then ask: “Am I going to go deaf?”
  • At the fourth question, after the examiner has put it, ask: “Can I still drive to work? And what do I do if it happens when I’m at home on my own?”

handover.label: Observations (practice nurse, today)
handover.result: Taken in the treatment room with lying and standing blood pressure. Mrs Smith is between attacks and feels well.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, HR 70 to 78 and regular, temperature 36.6 °C, capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L. BP 128/80 lying, 124/82 at 1 minute standing and 126/80 at 3 minutes, with no symptoms on standing. Every value is within normal adult ranges (white zone of the NSW Between the Flags adult chart if plotted), so no escalation is needed.
  • For Mrs Smith: there is no postural drop (a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic), so this is not orthostatic hypotension. A normal glucose and a regular pulse argue against a metabolic or rhythm cause. Together with the history, this is vestibular vertigo, not presyncope.
  • What it changes: she is well and stable, and can be managed in general practice with a planned ENT referral.

handover.label: Audiology report (this afternoon)
handover.result:
Diagnostic audiological assessment: pure-tone audiometry (air and masked bone conduction), speech audiometry, tympanometry and acoustic reflexes.

Clinical details: 55-year-old woman with two episodes of spontaneous rotatory vertigo over 3 months, each about 8 hours, with right-sided tinnitus, aural fullness and fluctuating hearing. Currently between episodes.

Otoscopy: clear canals, intact tympanic membranes on both sides.

Pure-tone thresholds (dB HL):

Frequency (Hz)2505001000200040008000
Right, air504535202530
Right, bone (masked)no response at 45 (limit)*45352025not tested
Left, air101010152530
Left, bone1010101525not tested

* Bone conduction at 250 Hz limited by equipment output; no air-bone gap at 500 to 4000 Hz.

Speech audiometry: word recognition 88% in the right ear (at 80 dB HL) and 100% in the left ear (at 55 dB HL).

Tympanometry: type A on both sides (middle ear pressure −10 daPa right and −15 daPa left (normal +50 to −100 daPa); compliance 0.6 mL right and 0.7 mL left (normal 0.3 to 1.6 mL)).

Acoustic reflexes: ipsilateral and contralateral reflexes present on both sides, with no reflex decay.

Conclusion: moderate low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear (250 to 500 Hz), mild at 1000 Hz, with good word recognition. Mild symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural loss in both ears (4000 to 8000 Hz), in keeping with age. Normal middle ear function on both sides. The asymmetric low-frequency loss fits the history of episodic vertigo with right ear symptoms. An asymmetric sensorineural loss warrants ENT review, with consideration of an MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude retrocochlear pathology. A repeat audiogram is recommended at ENT review to document any fluctuation.
handover.model:
• Read: in the right ear, air and bone thresholds match from 500 to 4000 Hz (no air-bone gap; bone at 250 Hz is at the equipment limit), so the loss is sensorineural. It is moderate at 250 to 500 Hz, about 35 to 40 dB worse than the left, and recovers by 2000 Hz: a low-frequency loss. Both ears share a mild high-frequency loss, which fits her age. Word recognition is good on the right. The tympanograms are type A and the reflexes are present, so the middle ear is normal.
  • For Mrs Smith: this confirms the bedside findings (Weber to the left with a positive Rinne: a right sensorineural loss). A low-frequency sensorineural loss in the symptomatic ear completes the criteria for definite Ménière's disease. Good word recognition and present reflexes favour an inner ear cause over a nerve lesion. The loss is still asymmetric, though.
  • What it changes: ENT referral with this report. ENT may arrange an MRI to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. This is a baseline for tracking her hearing.

expect:
• Identify: medical student; Kathy Smith, 55.
  • Situation: two spontaneous attacks of spinning vertigo in 3 months, each about 8 hours, with right hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness and vomiting; well between attacks; fears brain cancer.
  • Background: otherwise well; HRT; smokes 10 a day again; a glass of wine a night; lives alone, recently divorced, unprotected sex with several partners; drives.

  • Recommendation: Non-urgent ENT referral (MRI for the asymmetry); short-course prochlorperazine; GP review in 4 weeks.

Most likely: Ménière's disease, right ear. For: two spontaneous vertigo attacks within 20 minutes to 12 hours (about 8 hours each), a documented right low-frequency sensorineural loss, fluctuating right hearing, tinnitus and fullness, and a normal examination between attacks.

  • Vestibular migraine: for: attacks last hours and her mother has migraines. Against: no headache, aura or light sensitivity, and a documented one-sided loss.
  • BPPV: against: not positional, lasts hours, Dix-Hallpike negative.
  • Vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis: against: recurrent discrete attacks, fully well between, no URTI.

1. Explain: an inner ear disorder, cause unknown, not cancer; no cure, but symptoms can be controlled; hearing may worsen over time.
  2. Tests and referral: no brain imaging from general practice; non-urgent ENT referral with the audiogram; ENT may arrange an MRI of the internal auditory canals.

  4. Prevention: low-salt diet, limit caffeine and alcohol, stop smoking. Betahistine or a diuretic may be tried, usually with ENT advice.
  5. Opportunistic: condoms and an offer of STI testing; brief smoking advice and a separate appointment; check cervical, bowel and breast screening.

She is responsible for telling the driver licensing authority if her condition affects her driving; review her against Austroads once the attacks are controlled.

ddx.dx: Ménière's disease of the right ear
ddx.for: Two spontaneous attacks of spinning vertigo lasting about 8 hours, fluctuating right hearing loss with tinnitus and fullness, a documented right low-frequency sensorineural loss, and a normal examination between attacks.
Recurrent attacks lasting hours, and her mother has migraines.
ddx.against: No headache, aura or light or noise sensitivity, and she has a documented one-sided low-frequency sensorineural loss.
The attacks are spontaneous, not positional, last hours rather than seconds, and the Dix-Hallpike test is negative on both sides.

ddx.for: Severe vertigo with nausea and vomiting, and hearing loss as in labyrinthitis.
ddx.against: Two separate attacks with full recovery between them, no recent URTI or fever, and a normal head impulse test, if performed.

ddx.for: A one-sided sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus in a 55-year-old.
ddx.against: The symptoms are episodic and the loss is low-frequency, with good word recognition, present acoustic reflexes and normal cranial nerves V and VII.

ddx.for: Vertigo with vomiting in a 55-year-old smoker.
ddx.against: The attacks lasted 8 hours each with full recovery, there are no neurological symptoms, the examination is normal and the ear symptoms point to the inner ear.

guide:
In Part 1, give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The candidate may describe each examination step briefly while the examiner gives the finding; Dix-Hallpike may be offered rather than performed (item 21). Mrs Smith gives her ear symptoms and nausea only when each is named. If she is asked an open question about other symptoms she replies “Like what?”. Item 8 is awarded if at least two systems beyond the ears are screened (ear symptoms are scored in item 6). The observations are summarised as normal in Part 1, and the full set is handed over in Part 2. If the candidate attempts HINTS or a head impulse test, give the normal result. They can be credited as part of item 18, but she is not in an acute continuous vertigo, so HINTS is not expected. The sexual history and screening are revealed only when asked.

In Part 2, hand over both results together and ask the four questions in order. Mrs Smith asks whether it is a brain tumour and whether she will go deaf while the candidate explains; score item 29 from that explanation, in the diagnosis or management answer. Score the opportunistic items (33) from the management answer or the fourth question, and the driving and safety items (36) from the fourth question. If the sexual history was not taken in Part 1, credit item 33.1 if the candidate raises sexual health and offers STI testing in Part 2.

A high-performing candidate pins down true vertigo, its duration and the lack of positional triggers, then asks directly about hearing, tinnitus and fullness. They screen for central red flags and take a sensitive sexual history. They perform otoscopy and the tuning fork tests, interpret Weber to the left as a right sensorineural loss, and check for nystagmus, cerebellar signs and Dix-Hallpike. In Part 2 they read the audiogram as a right low-frequency loss and apply the diagnostic criteria for Ménière's disease. They reassure her honestly that it is not cancer, explaining why ENT may still order an MRI. They plan ENT referral, short-course prochlorperazine and salt and caffeine advice, and pick up the smoking, sexual health and screening opportunities.

A borderline candidate accepts “dizzy” without clarifying it, misses the ear symptoms because they never ask about them specifically, or reads Weber to the left as a left-sided problem. They may order a CT brain, offer long-term vestibular suppressants, dismiss her cancer fear without explaining, or leave out driving and red flags.
explain:
First, what does “dizzy” mean?

Dizziness covers four different symptoms:

  • Vertigo: an illusion of movement, often the room spinning. It is vestibular.
  • Presyncope: feeling faint or lightheaded. It is cardiovascular or postural.
  • Disequilibrium: unsteadiness without a sense of spinning.
  • Non-specific lightheadedness.

Once vertigo is established, timing and triggers sort most causes:

  • Seconds, brought on by head position: BPPV, with a positive Dix-Hallpike test.
  • Spontaneous attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours with ear symptoms: Ménière's disease.
  • Spontaneous attacks of minutes to days with migraine features: vestibular migraine.
  • A single episode of continuous vertigo over days: vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis if hearing is also affected, or posterior circulation stroke. HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) helps tell these apart in a patient who has the vertigo at the time of examination.

Ear symptoms are easily missed unless you ask for each one: hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness.

Why Mrs Smith has Ménière's disease

Ménière's disease is an inner ear disorder associated with endolymphatic hydrops. Its cause is unknown. The Bárány Society criteria for definite Ménière's disease are:

  • two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo, each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours;
  • an audiometrically documented low- to medium-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the affected ear, on at least one occasion before, during or after an episode;
  • fluctuating aural symptoms (hearing, tinnitus or fullness) in that ear;
  • no other diagnosis that explains the picture better.

Mrs Smith meets every criterion. Over time the hearing in the affected ear can become permanently worse. Some people develop symptoms in the other ear.

Bedside hearing tests

In a sensorineural loss, Rinne stays positive (air louder than bone) and Weber lateralises to the better ear. In a conductive loss, Rinne is negative in the affected ear and Weber lateralises to it. Weber to the left with Rinne positive on both sides therefore means a right sensorineural loss. Normal otoscopy excludes wax, effusion and perforation.

The results

The observations are normal, with no postural drop, so this is not presyncope. The audiogram shows a right low-frequency sensorineural loss with no air-bone gap, alongside a mild symmetrical high-frequency loss that fits her age. Good word recognition, type A tympanograms and present acoustic reflexes favour a cochlear cause. A vestibular schwannoma typically gives a progressive, often high-frequency loss with disproportionately poor word recognition. Any asymmetric sensorineural loss still warrants ENT review, and an MRI of the internal auditory canals is the test that excludes a schwannoma. General practice does not need to arrange brain imaging; ENT decides on the MRI. Syphilis serology in her STI screen also covers otosyphilis.

Differentials

  • Vestibular migraine: the main mimic, especially with a family history of migraine. Look for headache, aura and sensitivity to light or noise.
  • BPPV: excluded by the lack of positional triggers, the long attacks and a negative Dix-Hallpike.
  • Vestibular neuritis: causes one prolonged attack, not discrete recurrences.
  • Posterior circulation TIA or stroke: must be considered in a smoker. Recurrent 8-hour attacks with full recovery, no neurological symptoms and a normal examination argue strongly against it.
  • Otosyphilis: a rare mimic of Ménière's disease. This is one more reason her STI screen should include syphilis serology.

Management

  • Explain and reassure: explain what Ménière's disease is, and address her fear of cancer honestly. It is most likely an inner ear condition, not a brain cancer; because the hearing loss is one-sided, ENT may arrange an MRI to rule out a rare, non-cancerous growth on the hearing nerve.
  • Acute attacks: rest lying still, and use a vestibular suppressant or antiemetic such as prochlorperazine, for short courses only. Prolonged use slows the brain's compensation. If seen during an attack with vomiting, prochlorperazine 12.5 mg IM can be given.
  • Prevention: reduce salt, caffeine and alcohol, and stop smoking. Betahistine or a diuretic may be tried, though the evidence for both is limited. Intratympanic and surgical treatments are reserved for attacks that do not respond, and are rarely needed.
  • Referral: non-urgent ENT referral with the audiogram.
  • Hearing and tinnitus: audiology support and hearing aids if the loss persists.

Opportunistic care

  • Sexual health: she has several partners and uses no condoms. Advise condoms and offer STI testing as set out in the ASHM guidelines: chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis B according to her immunity.
  • Smoking: she has restarted. Give brief advice (Ask, Advise, Help), refer to Quitline (13 7848), discuss pharmacotherapy, and book a dedicated appointment.
  • Cardiovascular risk: as a 55-year-old smoker she should have an absolute CVD risk assessment (Australian CVD risk calculator) at the follow-up visit. Review her HRT at the follow-up visit (indication, route and dose; transdermal oestrogen carries a lower VTE risk), given that she smokes.
  • Cancer screening at 55: cervical screening every 5 years (self-collection is an option), a bowel screening kit every 2 years, and a BreastScreen mammogram every 2 years.

Safety netting

  • Call 000: weakness or numbness, a drooping face, slurred speech, double vision or trouble walking. These suggest a stroke.
  • Same-day GP or ED: a sudden drop in hearing in either ear that does not recover (sudden sensorineural hearing loss needs prompt treatment), or vomiting with no fluids kept down.
  • Safety: unpredictable attacks make driving, ladders and swimming alone unsafe. She should not drive while an attack could start, and should arrange other transport to work until the attacks are controlled. She is responsible for telling the driver licensing authority if her condition affects her driving; review her against Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive once the attacks are controlled. Because she lives alone, she should keep a phone nearby.
  • Follow-up: STI results followed up by phone or a short visit within a week; GP review in about 4 weeks with a symptom diary; ENT appointment; written information.
points: Clarify what “dizzy” means first. True vertigo is vestibular, and its timing and triggers (seconds and positional, hours and spontaneous, or days and continuous) narrow the cause.
Ask about hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness one by one. Patients rarely volunteer them, and they turn episodic vertigo into probable Ménière's disease.

Definite Ménière's disease needs two or more spontaneous attacks of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, a documented low- to medium-frequency sensorineural loss, and fluctuating aural symptoms in that ear.
Weber lateralises away from a sensorineural loss and towards a conductive one. With Rinne positive on both sides, Weber to the left means a right sensorineural loss.

An asymmetric sensorineural loss needs ENT review, and an MRI may be needed to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. Tell the patient this honestly while reassuring them that Ménière's disease is not cancer.

Treat attacks with short courses of prochlorperazine and advise a low-salt diet with less caffeine and alcohol. Use the visit for opportunistic care: sexual health, smoking cessation and cancer screening.
